words.d: sound effects: short sounds for actions, like a coin pickup
the music written for a game or film
music that repeats smoothly with no gap
a short tune linked to one character or situation
a short burst of music for a moment, like level complete
phone vibrations you can feel as feedback
borrowed reference music used only during development

lessons.title: Sound can't wait until the end

cards.text: Music and sound change how an experience feels. Teams often leave them until the end because they need lots of coordination. **That's a mistake: plan audio early.**
Disney first made the Star Tours ride "realistic", with only engine sounds and the pilot's voice. In testing, it didn't feel like Star Wars. Adding the famous music fixed it.
Even early arcade beeps created memorable themes: Pac-Man, Donkey Kong, The Legend of Zelda.
A recognizable sound becomes a brand. Candy Crush's deep-voiced "Sweet!" and "Delicious!" are famous. Plan sound for the tutorial, rewards and ads from the start.
No theme, no dream.

check.q: What did Star Tours teach Disney?
options: Music made the ride feel like Star Wars
Realistic sound is always the best choice
Rides work fine without any sound at all
check.why: Without the music, the experience felt flat.

lessons.title: Rent the hit or own the score

cards.text: Music is either **licensed** (existing songs you pay to use) or **original** (written for your game). **Never ship music you don't have the rights to.**
In 2010, a licensed song cost about $2,500 to over $30,000, paid once. Original music usually means hiring a **music director**, who composes, records and prepares it.
You don't need to play an instrument. You need opinions and examples. Rogers gave his Maximo composer a mix tape of film scores that fit each level.
Live games run for years, so a song license that expires mid-life is a problem. Most F2P music is original or from royalty-free libraries. Check that every license covers ads and trailers too.

check.q: Why are licensed hits rare in F2P games?
options: Live games run for years; licenses expire
Players dislike hearing famous songs
Phone speakers can't play them well
check.why: An expired license can force you to remove music from a running game.

cards.text: To direct music, you need **the words** to say what you want, plus **reference tracks** to show it.

Four groups of music words:
- **Time:** beat, tempo, rhythm
- **Height:** pitch, octave, chord
- **Colour:** instrument, tone, mood, theme
- **Loudness:** volume
Build a **temp soundtrack**: existing tracks that show the feel you want. Pick a style that fits your genre, or break the rules: sci-fi with polka?
Soft launch puts real builds in real countries. A forgotten temp track there is a real copyright problem. Label every temp file clearly, like TEMP_.
Time, Height, Colour, Loud.

check.q: What is a temp soundtrack for?
options: Showing the composer the feel you want
Shipping as the music in the final game
Testing the speakers on different phones
check.why: Examples remove guesswork, but temp music must never ship.

cards.text: List **every place that needs music**, then decide what you can afford. **Put your best piece on the start screen.**
Each level usually needs background music that **loops** without a gap. To save money, reuse tracks: in Maximo vs. Army of Zin, each world alternated two songs, so you never heard one twice in a row.
Don't forget the extras: title screen, pause menu, game over and minigames.
The home screen is your title screen, and players hear it thousands of times. Make it great but not tiring. Remix the main theme for holidays: cheap freshness for events.

check.q: Where should your best music go?
options: The start screen
The pause menu
The credits
check.why: It's the first music players hear, so it sets the mood.

cards.text: A **dynamic score** changes with the action: mystery, warning, combat, chase, victory. A **leitmotif** gives a character or situation its own tune.
Star Wars gives Darth Vader, Luke and Yoda each a theme. Hear the tune and you know who's coming.
Rogers' key rule: **make the music more exciting than the action on screen.** In Peggle, hitting the last peg plays Ode to Joy with fireworks. A tiny ball becomes a stadium moment.
The cheap mobile version: add instrument layers as a combo grows or time runs out. Gacha games give heroes a signature tune in their reveal trailer.
Music is the hype man. A good hype man is a little louder than the rapper.

options: A tune tied to a character or situation
A sound effect played on every button
A silent moment before a big reveal
check.why: Like Darth Vader's theme, it tells you who or what is coming.

cards.text: Sometimes the best "music" is the world itself, and sometimes it's **silence**.
Every place has its own sounds: a graveyard at night, a city at lunch. Maximo used world sounds in hub areas to set the mood, and normal music in the action levels.
Silence or a drumroll right before a chest opens makes the reveal explode. Then a different sound for each rarity tells players what they got before they read it.
Farm and village screens feel alive with birds, wind and chatter, without music fatigue. A quiet, gentle sound on failure keeps frustrated players from rage-quitting.
The drop is only epic because of the pause before it.

check.q: Why add silence before a reward reveal?
options: It makes the payoff feel bigger
It saves memory on older phones
It hides loading delays and bugs
check.why: Contrast makes the reveal sound land harder.

cards.text: Sound effects are **feedback**. Build the sound list together with the characters' moves, and make every action audible.
Sounds that go **up** in pitch feel good: extra life, task complete. Sounds that go **down** feel bad: failure, damage. Players feel it without thinking.
Realistic sounds ground the world but can be too quiet. Cartoony sounds are great for pickups and extra lives, but can break the mood.
Mobile sound lists are full of interface sounds: taps, swipes, matches, merges, coins, chest opens, errors. Vary the pitch slightly so the 10,000th coin doesn't drive players mad.

check.q: Which direction should pitch go for a good moment?
options: Up
Down
It doesn't matter
check.why: Rising pitch feels positive. Falling pitch feels like failure.

cards.text: Real recordings often sound wrong in a game. **Sweeten** them: mix sounds until they feel right.
Rogers found that breaking bones sound like dry twigs. His team added a bowling ball smashing into pins.
Lock the animation timing first, then fit the sound to it. A sound shouldn't end before the move, or keep going after it.
Sound can warn and guide. A falling bomb whistles so you can dive for cover. A crackle makes players pause before a magic door. Always check the copyright on any sound you use.
Remember the bowling-ball bone: right beats real.

options: Mixing sounds so it feels right
Making the sound much quieter
Adding soft music behind it
check.why: Real recordings can sound weak, so designers layer sounds.

cards.text: Too many sounds at once becomes noise. Sort every sound into **local, distant or priority**, so important sounds always cut through.

- **Local:** heard up close, fades with distance, like a ticking clock
- **Distant:** heard from far away, like explosions
- **Priority:** always plays, because it's gameplay feedback, like losing health
Name files so anyone can find them: a pattern like sfx_ui_button_tap_01 or mus_event_winter_loop.
Phones can play only a few sounds at once on tiny speakers. Limit repeats (for example, three coin sounds at a time) and lower the music under important feedback.
Local whispers, distant shouts, priority is the referee's whistle.

options: Priority sounds, like losing health
Distant sounds, like explosions
Background music in every scene
check.why: Priority sounds are gameplay feedback the player must hear.

lessons.title: If it only beeps, it's a secret

cards.text: Whole genres are built on music, from Dance Dance Revolution to Band Hero. But **never rely on sound alone: echo every audio cue with visuals.**
Visual echoes give extra clues, and they make the game playable for players who can't hear.
Mobile rhythm games like Beatstar and Piano Tiles-style games need sound on, so they say so on the first screen.
Many mobile players are muted. Every sound cue, like a timer ending or a rare drop, needs a visual or vibration twin.

check.q: Why echo audio cues with visuals?
options: Muted and deaf players still get the cue
Visuals are cheaper to make than sounds
Sound is too slow to react to on phones
check.why: A cue that only beeps is invisible to anyone who can't hear it.

cards.text: On phones, design **sound-off first**, then make sound-on delightful. Many players play muted: on the bus, in bed, in class.

- Every important event needs a clear visual signal.
- Let players keep their own music or podcast playing.
- Offer separate music and sound toggles, and remember the choice.
- Add captions for voice lines that matter.
Vibration is "sound you feel", and it works on mute. Light taps for buttons, medium for matches, heavy for big rewards.
Don't overdo vibration: it drains the battery and annoys. Always include an on and off switch.
Mute-proof, then make it sing.

check.q: What should mobile audio design assume first?
options: Many players have sound off
Everyone wears headphones
Players want loud music
check.why: If the game works muted, sound becomes a bonus instead of a requirement.

cards.text: Reward moments are where sound pays off most. **Bigger rewards get bigger, longer, higher sounds**, with particles and vibration.
Give level complete, chest open, rare reveal and rank-up each its own short sting. Each rarity tier gets a signature sound.
Ethics check: casino-style ringing on purchase or gacha screens can feel manipulative. Celebrate achievement, not spending.
Big downloads lose installs. Compress music, use mono for most effects, stream long tracks, and download extra audio after install.

options: Achievement, not spending
Every purchase, big or small
Losses, to soften defeat
check.why: Casino-like sounds on spending screens feel manipulative.
